hits.name: Charles Lamanna
hits.hook: Charles Lamanna: outage root cause, "deeply sorry", three factors behind the global gateway outage (647K, was 364K)
hits.text:
More details on the root cause can be found in the Microsoft 365 Admin center, and an abridged version can be found below. 

We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations. 

The incident on Thursday, November 12th, 2026, was caused by three main factors that together caused a global outage for the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services.

First, a latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers; neither the underlying defect nor the fix applies to broader Windows deployments.

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact.

Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

Second, a surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention. Within Microsoft 365, we maintain two independent and heterogenous network gateway systems designed for isolation and high availability. This allows many Microsoft 365 services to fail to/from them during outages or disruptions. Approximately fifteen hours before the outage, Teams failed over from the alternative networking gateway to the ‘primary’ gateway that also supports Exchange Online. This increased the load on the networking gateway and changed its traffic patterns. This type of failover is part of normal operations and is integral to standard Microsoft resiliency efforts.

Third, at the same time, nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day. This server capacity was on track to be returned to active service through routine maintenance and health processes. The service had sufficient capacity headroom, so the reduction in server capacity had no impact on its own.

Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July. This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States.

When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route users to other healthy endpoints. This happens often and is critical to avoiding any interruption due to hardware, software, or network defects and is normally what makes the service resilient. However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers. In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

Normally, the network gateway is composed of thousands of ‘capacity units’ which represent shards of capacity, hardware, and networking infrastructure. These ‘capacity units’ are then organized into regions. In this case, due to a separate issue, the normal bulkheads between these different partitions did not stop the cascading failure. This is what allowed the impact to spread across our network gateway infrastructure globally.

Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without issue for most of the outage. But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway.

Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again. Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.

After engineers confirmed the defect as the cause, we developed an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state. To effectively apply this fix, and to slowly bring the service online again, we took groups of servers out of service, applied the change, and restarted them before returning them to service. This process was carefully applied to large quantities of infrastructure at a time (e.g. 50%+ of a region).

The final Post-Incident Review (PIR) will provide more details later this week.

hits.text: I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code written by coding agents - here's a description of the external sandbox pattern, where agents run on your Mac but execute code in a WebAssembly or QEMU or Apple Container sandbox - with demos for Claude Code, Codex and Pi https://t.co/0XIhs4XYvQ
hits.original: I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code written by coding agents - here's a description of the external sandbox pattern, where agents run on your Mac but execute code in a WebAssembly or QEMU or Apple Container sandbox - with demos for Claude Code, Codex and Pi https://t.co/0XIhs4XYvQ
hits.draft_en:
Three of yesterday's best dev posts were the same idea.

GitHub: agent skills, write the instructions once and reuse them.
Simon Willison: let the agent run on your Mac, but execute its code in a sandbox.
Scott Hanselman: an MCP server for Windows Sandbox.

Reusable instructions + a box the agent can't break out of.

That's the Copilot Studio playbook too: knowledge and topics you reuse, actions you scope tight.
hits.video_tip: Vertical 12s: three screenshots stack on screen one by one (skills guide, sandbox diagram, Windows Sandbox), then an arrow points to a Copilot Studio agent with a 'scoped actions' label. Caption: 'Instructions in, blast radius down.'

drafts.rides: your own "Please contact your administrator" post (60,489 views, 5,183 likes, your best original in weeks) + Ignite day
drafts.text:
60,489 people saw my "Please contact your administrator" post.

Turns out a lot of us ARE the administrator.

So here's my Ignite wish list from the admin seat:

- error messages that say which policy blocked you
- agent permissions you can read in one screen
- admin controls that ship the same day as the feature

Show me that and I'll stop turning things off and on.
drafts.video_tip: Vertical 10s: you at your desk reading a 'Please contact your administrator' popup, slowly turn to the camera, point at yourself. Cut to the 3-line wish list typed on screen. Caption: 'I am the administrator.'

drafts.rides: @simonw external sandbox pattern (54.6K) + @github agent skills guide (50.4K) + @shanselman MCP server for Windows Sandbox (21.8K)
drafts.text:
Three of yesterday's best dev posts were the same idea.

GitHub: agent skills, write the instructions once and reuse them.
Simon Willison: let the agent run on your Mac, but execute its code in a sandbox.
Scott Hanselman: an MCP server for Windows Sandbox.

Reusable instructions + a box the agent can't break out of.

That's the Copilot Studio playbook too: knowledge and topics you reuse, actions you scope tight.
drafts.video_tip: Vertical 12s: three screenshots stack on screen one by one (skills guide, sandbox diagram, Windows Sandbox), then an arrow points to a Copilot Studio agent with a 'scoped actions' label. Caption: 'Instructions in, blast radius down.'

drafts.rides: @OpenAI embedded assessments (994K, up from 163K) + @gdb launch post (79K)
drafts.text:
OpenAI is giving outside experts deep access to its internal models to test the safeguards.

Now ask yourself: who has ever tried to break your Copilot Studio agent?

Not the maker. Someone else.

Give one colleague 30 minutes and a single goal: make it leak, overreach or lie.

Cheapest security review you'll ever run.
drafts.video_tip: Vertical 10s: hand a laptop to a coworker with a sticky note 'Break it', timer starts, show them typing a sneaky prompt into a test agent. Caption: 'Red team your own agent.'

Everything else is a demo until it ships to my tenant.

drafts.text:
Microsoft says Copilot is more cost effective than the other leading tools.

Cost effective only counts if you use what's in the license.

Example: Microsoft 365 Copilot includes 20 hours of Teams interpretation per month. Most people I ask have never turned it on.

Scheduled meeting, Interpreter on, pick your language. Done.
